Little
lĭt'-l
adj. (small in size, quantity, or degree; rendering Hebrew qaton, me'at, Greek mikros, oligos)
From Saxon lytel, small. Scripture uses the word as a term of tenderness (little children, little flock), of rebuke (little faith), and of method (here a little, and there a little) — and all three assume God does not despise the small.

Biblical Definition

Little in Scripture is rarely a dismissal. Our Lord makes smallness the condition of entry: “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3). What is required is not the innocence of children, which they do not have, but their dependence, which they cannot hide. The word is also the Shepherd's address to a frightened congregation: “Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). The two halves of that verse should be held together — a flock small enough to be afraid, and a kingdom given because it pleased the Father to give it. Nothing in the transaction depends on the size of the flock. There is a rebuking use as well: “Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith?” (Matthew 8:26). The faith is real, or He would not call it faith; it is little, and littleness of faith shows itself in fear during storms rather than in doctrinal error during calm. Finally the word describes God's ordinary pedagogy: “precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little” (Isaiah 28:10). Even where Isaiah reports it as the mockery of drunkards imitating a prophet's plodding speech, the method stands — God teaches His people in small increments, and the men who found it tedious were destroyed by what they would not learn slowly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Small in size, quantity, or degree; and by extension slight or of small dignity. Scripture makes littleness the posture of entry into the kingdom, the description of a flock given a kingdom anyway, and the measure of a faith that fears in storms.

expand to see more

LITTLE, a. [Sax. lytel; D. luttel.] Small in size or extent; not great or large; as a little body; a little animal.

2. Short in duration; as a little time; a little while.

3. Small in quantity or amount; as a little food; here a little, and there a little. Is. 28.

4. Of small dignity, power or importance. When thou wast little in thine own sight. 1 Sam. 15.

5. Slight; inconsiderable; as a little faith. O ye of little faith. Mat. 8. Little ones, young children; used also of the humble and dependent whom Christ forbids to offend.

Key Scripture

Matthew 18:3 — "And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven."

Luke 12:32 — "Fear not, little flock; for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom."

Matthew 8:26 — "And he saith unto them, Why are ye fearful, O ye of little faith? Then he arose, and rebuked the winds and the sea; and there was a great calm."

Isaiah 28:10 — "For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little:"

Modern Corruption

An age that measures everything by scale has made littleness a problem to be solved — the small church, the small family, the unnoticed obedience — when Scripture makes it the ordinary shape of the kingdom's work.

expand to see more

The pressure is felt most by pastors of small congregations and by fathers of ordinary households, and it is rarely stated as doctrine because it does not have to be. It arrives as a metric: attendance, reach, growth rate, the assumption that a faithful work will visibly enlarge and that one which does not has failed. Luke 12:32 is addressed to exactly this fear. The flock is little — Christ concedes the size rather than disputing it — and the kingdom is given not because the flock has grown but because it is the Father's good pleasure. A man who believes that verse can labour thirty years in a village and die without a metric to show, and have lost nothing. A man who does not will eventually change his message to fill his room.

The corresponding discipline is Isaiah 28:10, and it cuts against impatience in the same way. God builds by precept upon precept and line upon line, here a little and there a little — catechism, family worship, the same commands repeated to the same children, the Lord's Day arriving again. This is the method the mockers in Isaiah found risible, and it is the method that raises a household in the faith. The principle to recover is that in the kingdom the small is not the preliminary stage of the large; it is the unit of the work. A mustard seed, a cup of cold water, a widow's two mites, five loaves — the pattern is unbroken, and it is always the Lord who supplies the increase, which is precisely why the size of what He is given has never been the point.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qaton (small, young, insignificant) and me'at (a little, few); Greek mikros (small), oligos (few, little), and the compound oligopistos, of little faith.

expand to see more

Hebrew qaton (H6996) — small, young, of no account; used of the least in a household and of Saul when he was little in his own sight.

Hebrew me'at (H4592) — a little, few, a small quantity; the word in “here a little, and there a little” (Isaiah 28:10).

Greek mikros (G3398) — small in size, age, or rank; the term behind the little ones Christ forbids His people to offend.

Greek oligos (G3641) — few, little, small; used of the little flock and of the few who find the narrow way.

Greek oligopistos (G3640) — of little faith; a compound our Lord alone uses, and always of disciples, never of unbelievers.

Usage

"“Become as little children” — the dependence required, not an innocence children do not have."

"“Fear not, little flock” — the size conceded, the kingdom given anyway."

"“Here a little, and there a little” — God's ordinary pace in teaching His people."
